record.program_name: Fairfield Inclusionary Housing Policy and in-lieu fee (nexus study complete, ordinance in revision; Housing Element Action 1.2; Council goal HS 1.1)
record.administering_agency: City of Fairfield Housing Services Department and Community Development Department
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Not yet adopted. Council budgeted $120,000 for the nexus study (vendor under contract FY23-24) and $100,000 for policy development (FY24-FY27). Progress: Council study session October 2024, developer meeting January 2025, draft market and feasibility studies and draft ordinance completed early 2025, draft ordinance study session planned May 13, 2025. March 2026 status: study completed, revisions underway based on developer feedback. Fee levels and set-aside percentages are not public.
record.affordability_requirement: Not set. Housing Element objective is an inclusionary program with an in-lieu fee option whose revenue flows to the Housing Trust Fund.
record.next_deadline: Unknown. Watch Fairfield City Council agendas for the revised draft ordinance in 2026-2027; Housing Element timeframe was adoption by end of 2025.
record.layering_notes: Currently Fairfield's only existing production requirement is the Below Market Rate Program in the Housing Element resource list: 10% of detached homes in Residential Medium zones sold to moderate-income buyers with 45-year resale controls. An adopted inclusionary fee would capitalize the Housing Trust Fund (record above) and change underwriting for mixed-income rentals. Vallejo is adopting its ordinance (Chapter 16.216) in November 2026; Vacaville and Suisun City have only study programs. City pages 403; status read from the City's Council Goals performance reports.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. This program is a requirement imposed on private development and provides no public funds, so it does not itself trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing on the project.

record.program_name: Fairfield affordable housing Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Chapter 5, Article I), Fee Credit Bank and Train Station Specific Plan fee reduction
record.administering_agency: City of Fairfield Community Development Department (Director approves deferrals and fee credits)
record.typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver: affordable projects defer certain building and development fees to certificate of occupancy or permanent financing. Fee Credit Bank: credits from demolished buildings (water and sewer connection fees, not school or Solano County public facilities fees) can be applied to affordable projects. Train Station Specific Plan area: 25% reduction in development fees for multifamily units above 24 units per acre. ADUs under 750 square feet exempt from park, Cordelia open space, sewer connection and County public facilities fees; all ADUs exempt from a long list of City fees. No published dollar value of deferrals.
record.affordability_requirement: Deferral: multifamily must be at least 50% moderate-income and 25% low-income units, 55-year rental covenant (45 years ownership). Fee credits: low- and moderate-income units with a covenant of up to 55 years.
record.next_deadline: Apply to the Community Development Department with the building permit; no cycle. The City was updating its AB 1600 traffic and Northeast (TSSP) fees in 2022-2023; confirm current fee schedule.
record.layering_notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but fees are still paid, so budget them. Fee credits are a real reduction when a demolition site has banked credits; ask the Director for the current bank balance. Solano County public facilities fees cannot be deferred or credited by the City (County record: no County waiver program). A fee credit or reduction is public funds under Labor Code 1720(c) if above de minimis, hence unclear. Source is the HCD-posted October 2022 review draft of the 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted February 7, 2023, certified April 10, 2023 per the City's housing element site, not opened); Chapter 5 of the Municipal Code itself is on a blocked code host.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific rule found. The source (Fairfield 2023-2031 Housing Element review draft, Chapter 5 fee discussion) describes the Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Ch. 5, Art. I), Fee Credit Bank and Train Station Specific Plan fee reduction but says nothing on prevailing wage. Under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) fees reduced, waived or forgiven by a city are public funds; an interest-free deferral may also count. Coverage then depends on 1720(c) facts: (c)(3) de minimis test (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost) and (c)(5) affordable housing exemptions. Outcome depends on project facts, so left unclear (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720).
record.audit_note: Tier 3: prevailing wage left unclear; only basis is the general Labor Code 1720(b)(4) public-funds definition, and coverage turns on the 1720(c)(3) de minimis test and 1720(c)(5) exemptions for the specific project. Note: layering_notes cites 1720(c) for public funds; the operative definition is 1720(b)(4).

record.program_name: Vallejo Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 16.216, Affordable Housing Requirements; Housing Element Program B 2.1.1)
record.administering_agency: City of Vallejo Planning and Development Services Department, Long Range Planning (Hector Rojas, 707-553-7283)
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Introduced October 27, 2026; Council directed the Planning Commission version: applies to residential projects of 10 or more units; rental projects provide 4% affordable (2% very low, 2% low); ownership projects of 10 to 100 units 7% (4% low, 3% moderate), over 100 units 10% (6% low, 4% moderate). Staff had proposed a 20-unit threshold with 5% rental (1% VLI, 4% LI). In-lieu fee may be paid for some or all units, set by a later Council resolution and deposited in a separate City affordable housing fund; fractional units under 0.50 may be paid as fee. Alternatives: off-site units in the same census tract, rental units in ownership projects. EPS feasibility (March 13, 2026) found a subsidy gap of about $369,000 per very low-income apartment and $471,614 per low-income single-family unit, which are the equivalent in-lieu fee ceilings. Effective 90 days after final passage. Exemptions: disaster rebuilds, ADUs, residential care facilities, applications complete before the effective date.
record.affordability_requirement: Rental units at 30% of HCD income limits less utilities (2026 Solano three-person limits: VLI $61,850, LI $98,950, MOD $134,550); 55-year minimum covenants for rental and ownership units; Affordable Housing Plan and recorded Affordable Housing Agreement required; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units.
record.next_deadline: Second reading and adoption scheduled November 10, 2026; in-lieu fee resolution to follow before the effective date (about February 2027). Planning Commission asked for annual reports and a new feasibility study about two years after enactment. A Commercial Linkage Fee ordinance is to be drafted after adoption.
record.layering_notes: Vallejo's RHNA is 2,900 units with 1,446 lower and moderate units still unmet after 2025. This is the first inclusionary ordinance in Solano County; its in-lieu fund will be a new, small local gap source alongside the Housing Successor LMIHAF (separate record). Developers of 10+ unit rentals should model 4% affordable units or the fee once set. Underwriting in Vallejo is weak (EPS found rental yields of 4.7% to 5.0% against a 5.5% threshold), so the fee is expected to be modest. Staff report and draft ordinance opened on the City's inclusionary project page.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; this inclusionary ordinance (Chapter 16.216) provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any public loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on a project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

record.program_name: Vallejo Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo
record.administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo acting as Housing Successor; City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department, 200 Georgia Street, 707-648-4507 (Alicia Jones, Housing Director)
record.typical_award_size: FY 2023-24 report (dated December 5, 2024): deposits $376,807, expenditures $2,404,145 (of which $2,403,420 for extremely low-income housing development), ending balance $605,550, LMIHAF loans and grants receivable $15,773,272, no real property held. FY 2022-23: deposits $1,747,828, no expenditures, ending balance $3,534,099, receivables $13,199,965. $182,210 of a 2015-16 $500,000 excess surplus transfer to HOME match remains encumbered. Four properties in the Long-Range Property Management Plan are used for affordable housing. FY 2024-25 report (due December 2025) not located.
record.affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1: at least 30% of expenditures for households at or below 30% AMI and no more than 20% for 60% to 80% AMI over each five-year period; 55-year rental covenants; excess surplus rules.
record.next_deadline: No NOFA; the Housing Authority board (City Council) commits funds project by project and reviews the annual report each December. Ask the HCD Department what the $2,400,000 FY 2023-24 commitment funded and what remains after the FY 2024-25 report.
record.layering_notes: After the FY 2023-24 spend-down the fund holds about $600,000 in cash and relies on loan repayments from a $15,800,000 portfolio of legacy redevelopment loans, so it is a small, lumpy source. Pair with Vallejo HOME and CDBG (separate record), Vallejo Housing Authority PBVs, CMFA bonds (county record: $75,750,000 Step Up Housing and $32,131,176 Sacramento Street Apartments issues) and TCAC. Housing successor funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable units paid for solely from Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund money; other funds in the deal decide coverage (see prevailing_wage_basis). The Dissolution Law housing obligations (Buchongo settlement, 425 units) are fully met. Report opened from the Vallejo Housing Authority news page.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Vallejo housing successor fund is a housing successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund; Labor Code 1720(c)(4) names only the former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund, not housing successor asset funds, and no local rule requiring prevailing wage on these loans was found. Qualifying below-market loans may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (at least 40% of units at or below 80% AMI for 20 years) and homebuyer assistance under 1720(c)(5)(C). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
record.audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on public-funds logic only; no program or local rule found, changed to unclear.

record.program_name: Vallejo CDBG and HOME entitlement funds (FY 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan, FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
record.administering_agency: City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department (HUD CDBG entitlement and HOME participating jurisdiction), 200 Georgia Street, 707-553-7204 (Chari Francisco)
record.typical_award_size: FY 2026-27: CDBG allocation $1,049,400 plus $380,000 prior-year resources; HOME $420,114.54 (the draft plan's resource table also shows $1,554,400 CDBG and $1,049,400 HOME, an internal inconsistency). Activities: program administration, HOME TBRA, first-time homebuyer assistance, microenterprise, housing rehabilitation loans and grants, social services, permanent supportive housing (Broadway Village and Blue Oak Landing), Homeless Navigation Center, street and sidewalk repairs, housing counseling. CDBG program menu includes Affordable Rental Housing Development. HOME-ARP allocation $2,213,960 (2022). The Broadway Project, a 47-unit PSH conversion at 2441 Broadway, received a $12,000,000 Homekey grant, $3,500,000 Solano County ARPA and about $643,000 in City opioid settlement funds, and opened in late 2025.
record.affordability_requirement: CDBG: 51% of units at or below 80% AMI. HOME: 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI, balance at 60% AMI (rental), 55-year City covenant on larger awards.
record.next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2027-28 Annual Action Plan cycle has not been posted on the Housing News page; in the prior cycle the needs hearing notice went out January 20, 2026 for a February 5, 2026 HCD Commission hearing, so expect the FY 2027-28 needs hearing around February 2027. Contact the department by January 2027 to request a HOME or CDBG set-aside.
record.layering_notes: Vallejo is the only HOME participating jurisdiction in Solano County, so it is the one city where HOME development loans are a city decision. Recent HOME money has gone to TBRA, homebuyer and rehab programs rather than multifamily; a developer must ask for a HOME or CDBG set-aside during the Action Plan process. Stack with the Housing Successor LMIHAF, Vallejo Housing Authority PBVs, CMFA bonds and TCAC. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Draft Action Plan opened from the City's Housing News page.
record.cycle_notes: Consolidated Plan adopted July 8, 2025 covers July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2030. Annual cycle: community needs hearing before the HCD Commission (February), draft Action Plan and public hearing (April), Council action (June), program year starts July 1. FY 2026-27 cycle: needs hearing February 5, 2026, public hearing April 23, 2026, Council action June 23, 2026. City main site moved to vallejo.gov (403 to automated access); the cityofvallejo.net mirror still serves the HCD pages.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

record.program_name: Vallejo Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers (December 2024 RFP, up to 200 PBVs)
record.administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo (HACV), City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department, 200 Georgia Street, 707-648-4507; PBV contact Rosanna Roldan 707-648-4373
record.typical_award_size: RFP issued December 10, 2024 (proposals due January 2, 2025) for up to 200 project-based vouchers for existing, substantial rehabilitation and new construction units within the city, with awards to more than one respondent; a prior RFP closed July 8, 2024 and two RFPs ran in 2019. Existing PBV sites listed: Avian Glen Apartments (25 family units) and Blue Oak Landing (74 special needs units); October 2025 PBV interest lists opened for Sereno Village, Avian Glen and the Vallejo Housing Collaborative. Public comments on the 2024 Administrative Plan were heard December 10, 2024.
record.per_unit_cap: HAP contract rent capped at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR.
record.affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at 30% AMI); PBV units capped at 25% of a building unless serving elderly, disabled or supportive-services households; project preferences for homeless referrals.
record.next_deadline: No RFP open as of November 2026; the Authority has run rounds roughly annually (2019, mid 2024, December 2024). Watch the HACV news page and PlanetBids portal 42510 for the next PBV RFP; HUD's 2026 guidance to pause new PBV commitments may delay it.
record.layering_notes: The 2024 round offered up to 200 PBVs, the largest project-basing opportunity in the county and the key operating subsidy for the Step Up Housing and Sacramento Street Apartments conversions financed with CMFA bonds (county record). The Authority was understaffed in 2024-2025, so allow time for HAP contract execution. PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of 9+ contract units. Opened the HACV Recent News page, which carries the RFP notices and PBV site list.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (HUD PBV development requirements, labor standards): for development activity (new construction or rehabilitation) involving nine or more PBV contract units, the owner and its contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages and the PHA monitors compliance; existing-housing PBV contracts with no development activity do not trigger it. The Vallejo Housing Authority December 10, 2024 PBV RFP (up to 200 PBVs) covers existing, substantial rehabilitation and new construction units, so awards to new construction or rehab of 9+ contract units carry Davis-Bacon. https://www.cityofvallejo.net/our_city/city_government/vallejo_housing_authority/about_us/recent_news https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.153

record.program_name: Vallejo Affordable Housing Incentives and density bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 16.214)
record.administering_agency: City of Vallejo Planning and Development Services Department, Planning Division
record.typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law applied: 5+ unit projects providing 20% lower income or 10% very low income units (and other 65915 categories) receive a 5% to 35% bonus (more under current state law), concessions and incentives, land donation and childcare bonuses, and SB 35 streamlining procedures (16.214.14). Section 16.214.07 states the City is not required to provide financial incentives, land, fee waivers or dedication waivers but may at its discretion; 16.214.08 notes financial incentives may trigger prevailing wage. Recorded Affordable Housing Agreement required (16.214.09).
record.affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 set-asides; recorded Affordable Housing Agreement with 55-year rental covenants.
record.next_deadline: Not applicable; file with the planning entitlement.
record.layering_notes: No local enhancement; the chapter text still cites the older 5% to 35% range, and the City defers to Government Code 65915 as amended. Once Chapter 16.216 (inclusionary) takes effect in 2027, inclusionary units can count toward density bonus set-asides per state law; confirm with Planning how the two chapters interact. Vallejo adopted its 2023-2031 Housing Element December 30, 2024 (certified the next day); no Prohousing Designation for Vallejo was found on HCD's lists. Read on the zoneomics code mirror.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) reaches only construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds, and 1720(c)(1) exempts private residential projects on private property unless built under an agreement with a state agency, redevelopment or successor agency, or local public housing authority; the density bonus itself (Gov. Code 65915 as applied by Chapter 16.214) provides no public funds, so it does not by itself trigger prevailing wage. Any public loan, grant, land write-down or fee waiver layered on a project is assessed separately under 1720(b). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720 Section 16.214.08 states financial and certain other incentives may require prevailing wages if state law requires. Section 16.214.14 also offers the Gov. Code 65913.4 (SB 35) streamlined path, and 65913.4(a)(8) requires prevailing wages for projects using that path unless they have 10 or fewer units and are not otherwise public works (65913.4(a)(9)). https://california.public.law/codes/government_code_section_65913.4
record.audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: kept false because the program is primarily density bonus; projects using the 16.214.14 SB 35 path must pay prevailing wages above 10 units.

record.program_name: Vallejo PLHA formula allocation and pending Commercial Linkage Fee
record.administering_agency: City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department (PLHA); Planning and Development Services (linkage fee)
record.typical_award_size: PLHA formula (HCD 2024-2028 NOFA): Vallejo CY 2024 $354,734, CY 2025 $379,973, five-year estimate $2,217,088. How the City programs PLHA was not found on its pages. Commercial Linkage Fee: per the City's project page, a draft ordinance will be prepared and released for public review after the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance is considered and potentially adopted; no fee level or date set. Inclusionary ordinance: Planning Commission recommended adoption September 9, 2026; Council directed revisions October 27, 2026; second reading scheduled November 10, 2026, effective 90 days after final passage.
record.affordability_requirement: PLHA: at or below 60% AMI for rental assistance unless the five-year plan targets higher; 55-year covenant for rental development. Linkage fee: not yet set.
record.next_deadline: PLHA allocations arrive annually from HCD; ask the City for its five-year PLHA plan. Inclusionary ordinance second reading scheduled November 10, 2026; the linkage fee draft follows with no date set.
record.layering_notes: About $360,000 to $380,000 a year, the largest city PLHA share in the county. Combined with the inclusionary in-lieu fund and LMIHAF it gives Vallejo three small local pots that could be pooled into a NOFA; none has been. PLHA states no wage rule of its own; construction use is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). The opened source is HCD's PLHA formula NOFA; the City's PLHA plan was not located on cityofvallejo.net.
record.cycle_notes: PLHA is an annual HCD formula allocation, not a City NOFA. The Commercial Linkage Fee is pending and has no fee schedule yet.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines and Formula Allocation NOFA contain no prevailing wage provision; the City has not published a PLHA plan, and the Commercial Linkage Fee is not yet adopted. https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf

record.program_name: Suisun City Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers (2023 RFP, up to 96 PBVs) and Almond Gardens Apartments
record.administering_agency: Suisun City Housing Authority (City Council plus two tenant commissioners), 701 Civic Center Boulevard; Jason Goltiao, Housing Program Manager, 707-421-7332, jgoltiao@suisun.com

The vouchers went to Almond Gardens Apartments (707-815 Almond Street, Harbor Park LLC): 97 new units (96 restricted at 30% to 50% AMI) replacing a condemned 51 to 52 unit complex, total cost about $66,126,000, estimated HUD PBV funding about $3,274,484 a year, CDLAC allocation of $30,276,660 in tax-exempt bonds through CMFA plus $2,917,820 annual federal and $5,994,579 state credits (December 11, 2024). NEPA FONSI June 26, 2025, release of funds about July 15, 2025; construction June 2025 to January 2027.
record.per_unit_cap: HAP contract rent capped at 110% of FMR or exception payment standard.

record.next_deadline: The 2023 PBV allocation is fully committed to Almond Gardens. A new 5-Year PHA Plan (July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2030) was heard March 18, 2025. Ask the Housing Program Manager whether any PBVs remain or a new RFP is planned; HCV waitlist is closed.
record.layering_notes: Suisun City's housing authority is small (HCV only) and its PBV capacity is tied up in one deal, so a second Suisun project would need Fairfield, Vacaville or Solano County Housing Authority vouchers (separate records), which do not cover Suisun City. Almond Gardens shows the Suisun stack: CMFA bonds, 4% and state credits, PBVs, City land and impact fee waiver (separate record). PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction of 9+ contract units. suisun.com returns 403 to scripts; the Housing Authority page was opened with WebFetch and the CTCAC staff report (treasurer.ca.gov) supplied the financing figures.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: 24 CFR 983.153(c) (HUD PBV development requirements, labor standards): for development activity (new construction or rehabilitation) involving nine or more PBV contract units, the owner and its contractors must pay Davis-Bacon wages and the PHA monitors compliance; existing-housing PBV contracts with no development activity do not trigger it. The Suisun City Housing Authority page says the 2023 PBV RFP covers existing, new or rehabilitated units and that Federal Labor Standards will apply to eligible projects; Almond Gardens (97 new units replacing a condemned complex) is new construction, so Davis-Bacon applies. https://www.suisun.com/Departments/Development-Services/Suisun-City-Housing-Authority https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/983.153

record.program_name: Suisun City land contribution and impact fee waiver for affordable housing (Almond Gardens; Successor Agency and Housing Authority property)
record.administering_agency: City of Suisun City, Suisun City Housing Authority and Successor Agency to the Redevelopment Agency (Bret Prebula, City Manager and Executive Director, 707-421-7300)
record.typical_award_size: Case by case, no ordinance. The CTCAC staff report for Almond Gardens (CA-24-602, December 11, 2024; 97 units, 96 restricted) lists Suisun City land at $850,000 and an impact fee waiver of $1,535,881 in both construction and permanent sources, alongside Citibank bonds, deferred developer fee and tax credit equity. The Housing Authority owned 707 Main Street and the Successor Agency 701, 711, 713 and 717 Main Street; the City announced on September 1, 2026 that 707 Main Street and two downtown parking lots transferred to California Forever in the first phase of a downtown sale agreed in June 2026.
record.affordability_requirement: Negotiated; Almond Gardens is 100% affordable (48 units at 30% AMI, 48 at 50% AMI) with a 55-year CTCAC term and Section 8 PBVs on all 96 restricted units.
record.next_deadline: No program or deadline. Any waiver or land write-down requires Council or Housing Authority action; Housing Element Program 1.B promises impact fee deferrals and density bonuses for mixed-use and residential projects in the Downtown Waterfront Specific Plan area.
record.layering_notes: Suisun City has no trust fund, inclusionary fee or LMIHAF report found online, so land and fee concessions are its only local contribution. The Main Street sales to California Forever entities (CF Suisun LLCs) may generate Successor Agency or Housing Authority proceeds; ask the City whether housing asset proceeds will be re-deployed. A fee waiver on a 97-unit project is public funds under Labor Code 1720(c), hence prevailing wage true (the project is also bond and credit financed). Source is the CTCAC report; the Housing Authority DDA and the May 26, 2026 staff reports were not opened (suisun.com 403; Granicus agenda PDF opened but attachments not).
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. City land at below fair market value is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(3) and the impact fee waiver under 1720(b)(4), and the 1720(c)(1) private-property exclusion does not cover a project on Successor Agency or Housing Authority land; whether Almond Gardens is a public work depends on the disposition terms and remaining 1720(c) exemptions. The CTCAC staff report (CA-24-602) states no wage term. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720

record.program_name: Suisun City Residential Density Bonus and Density Incentives (Municipal Code Chapter 18.47, Ordinance 743 of March 21, 2017)
record.administering_agency: City of Suisun City Development Services Department, Planning Division, 707-421-7335
record.typical_award_size: Applies to multifamily, live-work and mixed-use projects of five or more units; implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 set-asides and bonuses; 15% to 35% additional bonus for land donation (18.47.065); childcare facility bonus or concession (18.47.070); parking ratios on request (18.47.080). Section 18.47.075 lets the Planning Commission or Council grant a bonus greater than the chapter requires for qualifying projects.
record.affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 set-asides; 55-year rental covenants; density bonus agreement.
record.next_deadline: Not applicable; file with the planning application.
record.layering_notes: The 2017 chapter predates AB 1287 and other state changes; state law governs where the chapter is less generous, but 18.47.075 is a useful local hook for asking for more than the state formula. Housing Element Program 1.B adds priority processing, fee deferrals and density and intensity bonuses for residential and mixed-use projects in the Downtown Waterfront Specific Plan area, and Program 3.A promotes the density bonus and fee deferrals for special-needs housing. Read on the zoneomics code mirror; the City's code host returns 403.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

record.program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Davis Municipal Code Article 18.05, Ordinance 2646) and Rental Housing Inclusionary Guidelines (Resolution 25-002, in-lieu fee)
record.administering_agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Affordable Housing Manager Iris Grace and Director Dana Bailey; Community Development Department for entitlements
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of 20 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half low income and half very low income (ordinance adopted July 2023). Resolution 25-002 (adopted January 7, 2025, 4 to 1) set the in-lieu fee for non-discretionary rental projects at $250,000 per required affordable unit and $125,000 for a fractional unit when the whole units are built on site. Staff had proposed $608,000 per unit (cost of the most recent all-affordable project) and the Council rejected $369,000. The fee is indexed annually by the construction cost index with a one-time payment or a multi-year option at a 10-year net present value. Ownership projects have separate land dedication and in-lieu options approved case by case.
record.affordability_requirement: 15% of rental units (7.5% low income at 80% AMI and 7.5% very low income at 50% AMI) with long-term covenants; alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication, Project Individualized Plan) must deliver equivalent affordability value and discretionary projects need Council approval of the alternative.
record.next_deadline: None (ordinance). Council on December 16, 2025 directed staff to amend the land dedication option as soon as possible; an amendment requiring land dedicators to also provide funding was introduced in March 2026 per local coverage. A broader revision of the ownership inclusionary rules is in progress. Verify current text with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.
record.layering_notes: The ordinance is the engine behind Davis's two main local tools: in-lieu fees and negotiated contributions flow to the City Housing Trust Fund, and land dedication produces fully improved affordable sites (see the Housing Trust Fund and land dedication records). For a 100% affordable developer this means partnering with a market-rate applicant on a dedicated site, or seeking Housing Trust Fund gap money. Staff's October 21, 2025 informational report found production lagging RHNA and proposed a mandatory financial review when a developer claims infeasibility; Councilmembers asked staff to look at 10% extremely low income in place of part of the 15% requirement. Section 40.27.110 of the zoning code ties Article 18.05 to state density bonus law. Stack with county records: no Yolo County housing trust fund or county NOFA exists; Yolo County Housing project-based vouchers and the state CDBG and HOME competitions are the county-level layers. Access: cityofdavis.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and to WebFetch; the Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org open and were used. The Resolution 25-002 text (showpublisheddocument/20364) and the October 21, 2025 staff report could not be opened.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

record.program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Woodland Municipal Code Chapter 15.16, Ordinance 1662 of 2020) inclusionary requirements and in-lieu fee
record.administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019) with the Community Services Department
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Citywide outside the Spring Lake Specific Plan: for-sale and multifamily rental projects of 30 or fewer units are exempt; 31 to 80 units provide 5% low income units; 81 or more units provide 10% low income, reduced to 5% if the project is built at 95% or more of maximum allowed density; in Downtown, Corridor Mixed Use and Neighborhood Commercial areas projects of at least 10 units built at maximum density (and at least 10 units per acre) owe 5% for-sale units. Very low income requirements were dropped in the April 2020 amendments. Alternatives: land dedication valued at the in-lieu fee times required units, or in-lieu fees per an adopted fee schedule (reviewed annually) or, if none is adopted, as negotiated in the inclusionary housing agreement and paid before building permits. Example: Ashley and Main (168 units, 2020) paid $469,413. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Fund (Fund 1327); up to 10% of annual income may fund administration.
record.affordability_requirement: Low income (80% AMI) rental units must be permanently affordable; for-sale affordable units 10 years minimum reset at each resale with a $1,000 silent second and equity share; rents calculated at 50% AMI for very low and 80% AMI for low income units.
record.next_deadline: None (ordinance). The 2020 temporary relief provisions were set to expire in April 2022 unless dwelling unit goals were met; the Housing Element (Program A.27) committed to a LEAP-funded study of a standardized square-foot in-lieu fee, including nonresidential. Confirm whether a fee schedule has been adopted with the Housing Analyst.
record.layering_notes: Woodland's inclusionary program feeds the only local soft money in the city (Fund 1327, see the in-lieu fund record). Thresholds are generous to market-rate builders (exempt to 30 units, 5% at 31 to 80), so most revenue has come from Spring Lake development agreements and large projects. Spring Lake has its own stricter rules (separate record). Rental inclusionary units must accept Section 8 vouchers (Yolo County Housing PBVs can layer). Chapter 15.16 also now contains the City's state density bonus procedures. No county inclusionary applies inside city limits (Yolo County Chapter 8-8 is unincorporated only). ecode360 hosts the official Woodland code and opened directly.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

record.program_name: Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fees Fund (Fund 1327) and Spring Lake off-site fee revenues: City gap loans to affordable projects
record.administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department, Housing (Deputy Director Erika Bumgardner; Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019)
record.typical_award_size: Case-by-case residual receipts loans. Most recent: $1,500,000 to Yolo County Housing for Tupelo Family Apartments (73 units, 72 restricted, 30% to 80% AMI, Yolano-Donnelly Choice Neighborhoods early project), approved July 15, 2025 as a 55-year residual receipts loan at 3% simple interest with a 55-year regulatory agreement; about $20,833 per affordable unit, which staff compared with Mutual Housing at Spring Lake Phase I ($38,462 per unit) and Vista Del Robles Phase II ($41,667 per unit). Earlier the City lent $2,410,000 of in-lieu and Spring Lake off-site fees to Mutual Housing's farmworker phases (100 units) and granted $1.48 million plus free City land for the 61-unit East Beamer Way supportive housing campus. Fund balance not stated; staff noted that in-lieu receipts over the prior four years were enough to replace $500,000 of ARP funds.
record.per_unit_cap: None published; recent awards $20,833 to $41,667 per unit.
record.affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low and low income rental units with 55-year covenants; Council priority for projects leveraging tax credits, AHSC and other state funds.
record.next_deadline: No NOFA; developers request funding through Housing staff ahead of state or TCAC applications. Tupelo received a $27,999,100 AHSC award in December 2025 and will pursue tax credits in 2026 or 2027; staff planned a fall 2025 ARP spending plan update. Contact the Housing Analyst before an application round.
record.layering_notes: Woodland's pattern is a City commitment letter sized to make the AHSC or TCAC application competitive, with Yolo County Housing or Mutual Housing as developer and Sutter Health or Alta California Regional Center philanthropic layers (Tupelo also has $1.5 million from Sutter and $2.3 million from Alta). Loans are residual receipts and subordinate, so they fit under 4% bond deals. Fund revenue is lumpy (large projects and Spring Lake development agreements); confirm the balance before relying on it. Layer order: AHSC or MHP, 4% or 9% credits, Yolo County Housing PBVs, City Fund 1327, CDBG for off-site infrastructure. Agenda packets are on CivicClerk (woodlandca.api.civicclerk.com file streams open; the portal itself is a JavaScript app).
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. No City of Woodland Fund 1327 NOFA, guideline, resolution or loan term requiring prevailing wage was found (the July 15, 2025 Tupelo loan staff report and agenda packet contain no wage term for the loan). Loans are public funds under 1720(b)(1) or (b)(4), but qualifying below-market loans may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) and small subsidies under 1720(c)(3). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
record.audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on public-funds logic only; no program or local rule found, changed to unclear.

record.program_name: Development Impact Fee Deferral Program (MPFP fee deferral for multifamily, December 2008 ordinance) and case-by-case deferrals for affordable projects
record.administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department and Administrative Services (Finance)
record.typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver. Under Ordinance No. 1690 (adopted June 21, 2022, no expiration date) residential infill projects (single-family or multifamily on vacant or underutilized parcels in urbanized areas) may defer ten City impact and capacity fees (General City, Library, Police, Water Capacity, Roads, Administration, Storm Drain, Fire, Wastewater, Parks) under a recorded fee deferral agreement and lien; deferred fees are due at the earlier of the final inspection request or 12 months, at the rate in effect at permit issuance. Spring Lake Infrastructure Fees, permit and plan check fees and non-City fees are not deferrable. Approval by the City Manager or Council depending on amount. The Council has also approved case-by-case interest-free deferral to just before certificate of occupancy for affordable projects (Housing Element). The Prohousing application cites Vista Del Robles (72 units, 2024) as a user.
record.affordability_requirement: None for the general program; affordable projects may also get case-by-case Council deferrals.
record.next_deadline: Rolling, no deadline as of November 8, 2026. Apply through Community Development, (530) 661-5820.
record.layering_notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but is not a subsidy; combine with the density bonus fee waiver incentive and Fund 1327 loans. Woodland was designated Prohousing by HCD in 2025 (application March 21, 2025), which adds Prohousing points in state programs. Spring Lake has its own financing plan; Spring Lake Infrastructure Fees cannot be deferred.
record.cycle_notes: Ongoing program; apply to Community Development before permit issuance. Ordinance 1690 has no sunset (replaced the 2008 program that ran through June 30, 2022).
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts fees, loans or interest rates normally required that are reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven as public funds; an interest-free deferral of impact fees may fall within that language, and the deferral guidelines (Ordinance 1690) state no wage term. Coverage depends on the deferral terms, other public funds and 1720(c), including the 1720(c)(3)(B) de minimis test and 1720(c)(1) for private projects on private property. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
record.audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: false was not supported by a rule; 1720(b)(4) may reach fee deferrals, changed to unclear.

record.program_name: CDBG entitlement program (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, annual Action Plan NOFA) and PLHA formula allocation
record.administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department, Housing (Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019, franklin.cui@cityofwoodland.gov)
record.typical_award_size: FY 2025/26 CDBG allocation $473,643 (FY 2024/25 $475,086; FY 2026/27 estimated $443,278), about $2.4 million over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan adopted July 15, 2025. Allocation pattern: 65% public infrastructure (ADA Accessibility Project $307,868 in FY 25/26 and $299,622 in FY 26/27), 15% public services capped (about $55,000 to $66,000 to food, shelter and fair housing), 20% administration. The five-year plan budgets only $100,000 for the Improve Housing Access and Quality goal, so direct CDBG support to rental development is minimal; past awards funded shelters, supportive housing services and fair housing. HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA lists Woodland at about $1.09 million over five years. Woodland is not a HOME participating jurisdiction and applies to the state HOME competition (used for first-time homebuyer loans; the interest list is closed).
record.affordability_requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI or low and moderate income area benefit; state HOME at or below 80% AMI.
record.next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The City says it typically issues the CDBG NOFA in early winter with awards approved by Council in June or July; the FY 2027/28 NOFA is expected about mid February 2027 with applications due about mid March 2027.
record.layering_notes: Treat Woodland CDBG as a source for off-site infrastructure or ADA work adjacent to an affordable project rather than construction gap; the housing goal is $100,000 over five years. State HOME and PLHA are the city's other formula sources but have gone to homebuyer assistance; ask Housing staff whether PLHA could be redirected to a rental project. Yolo County's CDBG and HOME cover only unincorporated areas. Pair with Fund 1327 loans and Yolo County Housing PBVs. The CDBG page and DocumentCenter PDFs on cityofwoodland.gov open directly; some scanned PDFs (one-pager, SB 341 report) have no text layer.
record.cycle_notes: Annual CDBG NOFA; program year starts July 1. FY 2026/27 cycle: about $470,000 available, NOFA and applications posted February 18, 2026, applicant workshop March 11, 2026, applications due March 18, 2026 at 5:00 p.m., Council approval of the Action Plan July 21, 2026 (Resolution 8728).
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Federal rules by name: HOME, 24 CFR 92.354 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/24/92.354), Davis-Bacon wages apply when 12 or more units are HOME-assisted; CDBG, Housing and Community Development Act sec. 110 (42 U.S.C. 5310), Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-financed construction, and for residential property only at 8 or more units. Below those thresholds federal wages do not apply; state prevailing wage may still apply under Labor Code 1720 depending on 1720(c) exemptions (single-family rehab and homebuyer aid are exempt under 1720(c)(5)(C)).

record.program_name: Woodland Housing Successor Agency (former Redevelopment Agency) Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (SB 341 reporting)
record.administering_agency: City of Woodland as Housing Successor to the former Woodland Redevelopment Agency (Community Services and Community Development Departments)
record.typical_award_size: Small. The FY 2021/22 SB 341 report (dated August 1, 2022, the latest posted) shows a Housing Asset Fund ending balance of $51,025 cash (one loan payoff), no real property, five rental loans outstanding totaling $4,123,722 and seven first-time homebuyer loans totaling $674,693 (principal and interest through June 30, 2022). Unencumbered funds were under $1 million, so no excess surplus. Any future money comes only from loan repayments.
record.affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 targets: at least 30% of LMIHAF expenditures for rental housing at or below 30% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI, with 55-year covenants.
record.next_deadline: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No later SB 341 report is posted; ask Housing staff for the current balance.
record.layering_notes: Useful negative information: Woodland's post-RDA housing money is the inclusionary Fund 1327, not the successor fund, which held about $51,000 in cash at June 30, 2022. Rental loan repayments could add a small extremely low income layer over time. The SB 341 report is a scanned PDF; it was read page by page as images.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The Woodland housing successor fund is a housing successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund; Labor Code 1720(c)(4) names only the former redevelopment Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund, not housing successor asset funds, and no local rule requiring prevailing wage on these loans was found. Qualifying below-market loans may be exempt under 1720(c)(5)(E) (at least 40% of units at or below 80% AMI for 20 years) and homebuyer assistance under 1720(c)(5)(C). https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
record.audit_note: PW citation pass Nov 9, 2026: true rested on public-funds logic only; no program or local rule found, changed to unclear. The SB 341 report PDF has no text layer, so it could not be searched.

record.program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 15.40, Ordinance 14-4) with Housing Trust Fund Program in-lieu alternative and Urban Infill Area incentive
record.administering_agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta, (916) 617-4555)
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of 5 or more units citywide (adopted April 2014, replacing the redevelopment-area Chapter 15.10): rental projects set aside 10% of units (5% very low income, 5% low income); for-sale projects 10% low income, with rental units substitutable. Units on site, dispersed, at least 90% of the smallest market unit size, concurrent with each 25% of market units. Alternatives at Council discretion: payment into the Housing Trust Fund Program at the amount set in the Book of City Imposts Section VIII-N (a regional comparison in late 2025 listed West Sacramento's in-lieu fee at about $7,699 per dwelling unit, assessed per market-rate unit), acquisition and rehabilitation of market units, off-site construction, or preservation of at-risk units. Projects in the priority Urban Infill Area earn a discount on the in-lieu fee based on adjusted density (dwelling unit equivalents for structured parking, public open space and ground floor commercial). Incentives include reduced parking, priority processing, standards waivers and technical assistance; financial incentives only to the extent City programs exist.
record.affordability_requirement: Rental: 5% very low (50% AMI) and 5% low income (80% AMI) for 55 years; for-sale: 10% low income with a 45-year goal and recapture on early release.
record.next_deadline: None (ordinance). The Housing Element (Program HE-PR-1.2) commits to refining Chapter 15.40 to target lower incomes and reduce the burden on market-rate housing; six affordable housing agreements were approved 2018 to 2020. Confirm the current Book of City Imposts fee with the Housing Division.
record.layering_notes: The in-lieu alternative is the main revenue source for the City's Housing Trust Fund (Fund 261-9385), which funds gap loans (separate record). Because the per-unit fee is low relative to Davis ($250,000) and Folsom, most subdivisions in Southport pay the fee rather than build, so West Sacramento's affordable production comes from City-assisted 100% affordable projects in the Bridge District and Washington (West Gateway Place I and II, Landmark Lofts, the Grand Gateway 114-unit project). Overconcentration cap: no more than 40% of a project's units may be inclusionary. No county inclusionary applies inside the city. ecode360 hosts the official West Sacramento code and opened directly; cityofwestsacramento.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and WebFetch, and the Book of City Imposts could not be opened.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

record.program_name: Affordable Housing, Density Bonuses and Incentives (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 17.23, Ordinance 19-1)
record.administering_agency: City of West Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division
record.typical_award_size: Regulatory. Chapter 17.23 applies in all zones allowing residential use and grants qualifying developments and qualifying land transfers the density bonus, incentives and concessions specified in Government Code 65915 by reference (no local enhancement, no local cap). Requests are processed with the entitlement and approved if state criteria are met; a continued availability agreement is required before approval. Section 17.23.070 restates Housing Accountability Act limits on denying projects with at least 20% low income units. The 2019 zoning code update raised minimum and maximum densities in medium, high density and mixed-use zones (about 2,025 acres), so the Housing Element targets only about 5 density bonus units for the cycle.
record.affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, senior, 100% affordable) with covenants per Government Code 65915(c).
record.next_deadline: None; request in writing to the Planning Division with the project application. The City reviews the chapter in its biannual zoning code update.
record.layering_notes: West Sacramento's leverage is zoning (high base densities in the Bridge District, Washington and Pioneer Bluff specific plan areas, mixed-use and waterfront zones) rather than the bonus itself. SB 35 and now SB 423 streamlining accepted for 10% or more affordable projects. Chapter 15.40 incentives (parking reductions, priority processing, standards waivers) can be combined. The code mirror (zoneomics) matches ecode360's section list; confirm against the official code.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

record.program_name: West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (City-affiliated nonprofit co-developer and property owner)
record.administering_agency: West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (501(c)(3), EIN 94-3184534, 2950 Beacon Boulevard) working with the City Housing Division
record.typical_award_size: Partnership capacity rather than a funding program. The Housing Element names the West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (WSHDC) alongside Yolo County Housing as the City's standing nonprofit partners for pursuing state and federal funds (Programs HE-PR-1.6 and 1.9). WSHDC co-developed West Gateway Place (77 units, 2017, $29.8 million) and West Gateway Place II / The Bridge at West Gateway (60 units, 2025) with Jamboree Housing on City-contributed land, and owns scattered rental properties managed by a third-party manager.
record.affordability_requirement: Projects to date serve 20% to 60% AMI families with permanent supportive units; terms set by the City and state funding.
record.next_deadline: None; WSHDC has no NOFA. Approach through the City Housing Division when proposing a joint venture on City or successor agency land.
record.layering_notes: For an outside developer WSHDC is the local partner that unlocks City land, Housing Trust Fund and HOME program income commitments and local-nonprofit scoring; Jamboree has been its repeat co-developer. Mercy Housing (Esperanza Crossing, CMFA bonds) and New Hope CDC (9% award for a West Sacramento project) have also worked in the city without WSHDC. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the welfare exemption (county records). WSHDC has no website; corporate facts are from nonprofit registries and the Jamboree fact sheet.
record.audit_note: Audit 2026-11-08: funding_type stays other. WSHDC is a City-affiliated nonprofit partner with no deployable funds or NOFA, so no money enum fits; Housing Element Programs HE-PR-1.6 and 1.9 confirm its partner role and its work with Jamboree on West Gateway Place I and II.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. The West Sacramento 6th Cycle Housing Element (Programs HE-PR-1.6 and 1.9, https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/west-sacramento-6th-adopted071521.pdf) names WSHDC as a partner and states no prevailing wage rule. WSHDC is a nonprofit that supplies no public funds of its own, so the partnership does not itself trigger wages; City land contributed below fair market value is public funds under 1720(b)(3), and City Housing Trust Fund or HOME loans are tested under their own rules, where below-market residual receipts loans may fall under the 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption (below-market loan, at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI; see DIR PW 2019-018, https://dir.ca.gov/OPRL/coverage/year2020/2019-018.pdf) and HOME carries Davis-Bacon at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
